name: The Misinformation Effect
statement: Misleading information encountered after an event can distort a person's memory of what they originally witnessed.
meaning: The misinformation effect occurs when a person's recall of an event becomes less accurate because of information encountered after the event. Post-event details, especially from leading questions or others' accounts, get woven into memory. Elizabeth Loftus's research made it a cornerstone of the case against uncritical eyewitness testimony.
mechanism: Proposed accounts include the misleading and original information blending together, the misleading information overwriting the original, and source misattribution, in which post-event details are mistakenly remembered as part of the original scene. Because the misleading information is often more recent, it can be more easily retrieved and mistaken for a genuine memory.

examples.text: In Loftus and Palmer (1974), participants asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" gave higher speed estimates (about 40.8 mph) than those asked "hit" (about 34.0 mph), and were later more likely to falsely recall broken glass.
In a later slide study, participants given a post-event suggestion of a yield sign were more likely to report a yield sign when the original scene actually showed a stop sign.
A witness questioned with leading wording by investigators may incorporate suggested details, undermining the reliability of their later courtroom account.

whyItMatters: The effect has profound implications for the justice system, showing eyewitness memory is reconstructive and vulnerable to suggestion, contamination, and leading questions. It underpins reforms in police interviewing and lineup procedures.
limits: The effect's size varies with how the misinformation is delivered, the delay, and warnings; forewarned or attentive witnesses resist it better. It does not mean all memory is unreliable or that every recalled detail is false, only that memory can be distorted under identifiable conditions.
misreadings: It does not prove memories are freely fabricated at will; distortion typically requires specific misleading post-event input, not mere passage of time.
origin: Elizabeth Loftus, foundational studies in the mid-1970s, notably Loftus and Palmer (1974).

sources.text: Wikipedia's "Misinformation effect" article — supports the definition that post-event information reduces recall accuracy, the blending/overwriting and source-misattribution mechanisms, and Loftus's central role.
Simply Psychology's "Loftus and Palmer (1974)" — supports the smashed/hit speed-estimate findings and the false recall of broken glass demonstrating reconstructive memory.
